title: Stack
tagline: LIFO stack operations, array implementation, underflow and overflow, and stack applications such as bracket matching and postfix evaluation.

overview.intro: A stack is one of the simplest and most useful data structures because it models reverse-order and nested processing directly. This chapter explains what a stack is, what its operations do, how it is commonly implemented with an array and a top pointer, and why it is a good fit for tasks like bracket matching and postfix evaluation. It also covers the boundary cases of underflow and overflow, and it contrasts a stack with a queue so that you can choose the right structure for a given job.

blocks.text: A stack is a data structure that stores values and lets you remove only the value that was added last. It is often described as LIFO, which stands for last in, first out. The two main operations are push, which adds a value to the top, and pop, which removes and returns the top value. There is also an operation to read the top value without removing it, sometimes called peek. You can think of a stack like a pile of books: you put a new book on top, and you can only take the top book off next. That is the wrong mental model if you think the next grab must always be the newest item, but that is exactly what LIFO means in this context.

A stack is not the right structure for every job. If you need to remove the value that was added first, a stack is a poor fit because it removes the value that was added last. If you need to remove a value from the middle, a stack is also a poor fit because it only gives you access to the top. What a stack is good for is situations where the most recent addition is the next one to be processed. That situation appears whenever work is nested or deferred, such as matching brackets, managing method calls, or evaluating certain kinds of expressions.

learn.title: The basic operations: push, pop, peek

blocks.text: The three core operations are push, pop and peek. Push adds a new value to the top of the stack. Pop removes the top value and gives it back. Peek looks at the top value without changing the stack. If you define these operations, you should also handle the cases where the stack is empty. Popping from an empty stack is an error called underflow. If the stack has a fixed size and you try to push when it is already full, that is overflow. A well-defined stack implementation must say what happens in these cases rather than assume they never occur in an examination program.

Overflow is what happens when you push onto a full stack.

learn.title: Implementing a stack with an array

blocks.text: One common way to implement a stack is with an array and a separate variable that remembers where the top is. The array gives you a fixed amount of space, and the top variable tells you where the next push should go and where the next pop should read from. Each push moves the top variable to the next slot and stores the new value there. Each pop reads the value at the top and then moves the top variable back. This is simple and fast for the stack operations, because both push and pop only touch one end of the structure.

The trade-off is that an array-based stack has a fixed capacity. If you need more values than the array can hold, you get overflow. If you know in advance that the stack will never need more than a certain number of values, an array can be a perfectly reasonable choice. If you do not know the maximum size, you may prefer a different implementation. The syllabus does not require you to memorise a single implementation detail, but it does expect you to understand the idea that a stack is usually built so that it only touches one end of the structure.

items.note: The top is now 30. The array slots above the old top are no longer part of the stack.
You get 30 back, and the new top becomes 20.

learn.title: Why stacks are useful: reverse order, nesting, and matching

blocks.text: Stacks are most useful when the job requires reverse order. If something arrives and then needs to be handled in the opposite order, a stack does that naturally. This is why stacks are associated with reversing sequences, with nested structure, and with situations where you need to remember what came most recently and come back to it later. A simple example is a pile of tasks where the latest task is the one you want to handle next. Another is matching opening and closing brackets: every opening bracket is remembered until its matching closing bracket appears.

Postfix notation is a notation where operators come after their operands. Evaluating a postfix expression is a classic stack application. You read the expression left to right, push values onto the stack, and when you reach an operator you pop the needed operands, combine them, and push the result back. The stack is exactly the structure that keeps the intermediate results in the right order. This is a frequent examination topic because it shows why a stack is not just an arbitrary data structure but the right one for a specific computational pattern.

items: A stack reverses order: the most recent item is handled first.

learn.title: Underflow, overflow, and the empty-stack case

blocks.text: Underflow and overflow are not just implementation annoyances; they are part of understanding what a stack is. Underflow means you tried to pop from a stack that has nothing on it. Overflow means you tried to push onto a stack that cannot hold any more values in the implementation being used. In a fixed-size array implementation, overflow happens when the stack is full. In an implementation with dynamic space, overflow is less of a practical problem, but the idea still matters because you need to decide how the stack behaves at its limits.

Examination questions often include these boundary cases on purpose. A stack program that works for a few values can fail silently or crash when it reaches the empty or full case unless the boundary is handled. So when you write or trace a stack program, always ask what happens when the stack is empty before the first pop and what happens when it is full before the next push. That habit is part of what examiners are usually looking for when they ask about stack implementations.

learn.title: Stack versus queue: the access-order difference

blocks.text: A stack and a queue are not the same thing, but they are easy to confuse because both store a sequence of values and both restrict how you access them. The difference is the order. A stack removes the most recently added value first. A queue removes the least recently added value first. That single difference is what determines which one is appropriate. If you are modelling a pile of plates, the most recent plate is the next one to be taken, so a stack is a good match. If you are modelling a line of people waiting for service, the first person to arrive is the first to be served, so a queue is a much better match.

This difference also makes each structure awkward for the other’s job. If you need to remove the earliest-added value, a stack is the wrong tool because it keeps giving you the latest value. If you need to remove the latest-added value, a queue is the wrong tool because it keeps giving you the oldest value. Knowing why a structure fits or does not fit a task is often more important than knowing the definition of the structure itself.

items: A stack is LIFO: last in, first out.
A queue is FIFO: first in, first out.
A stack suits nested or reverse-order processing.
A queue suits waiting in arrival order.
Picking the wrong structure is a common source of awkward code.

items.meaning: The order in which a data structure allows removal or access to its values.

learn.title: Stack in the context of the 2027 Computer Science syllabus

blocks.text: In the 2027 ISC Computer Science syllabus, the stack is part of the Data Structures section. The syllabus expects you to understand the basic idea of a stack, its operations, and the situations it suits, especially bracket matching and postfix evaluation. It also expects you to distinguish a stack from a queue and to understand underflow and overflow as boundary cases. The emphasis is on understanding why the structure works the way it does, not on memorising a single code template for all possible uses.

That means you should be able to describe what push, pop and peek do, explain what underflow and overflow mean, trace a short stack computation, and say why a stack is a good or bad fit for a given problem. You do not need to guess at advanced stack variations that are not part of the syllabus. If a question goes beyond the syllabus expectations, the safest move is to work from the core ideas you do know rather than invent extra rules.

items: Know the stack operations and their effects.
Know what underflow and overflow mean.
Be able to trace a small stack computation.
Know the main stack applications mentioned in the syllabus.
Be able to compare a stack with a queue.
